story: Imagine a region of space so empty that it defies cosmic logic. Discovered in 1981 by Robert Kirshner and his team during a galactic redshift survey, the Boötes Void is a mind-bogglingly vast expanse of nothingness. Spanning up to 330 million light-years across and centered 700 million light-years from Earth, this 'Great Nothing' is one of the largest supervoids in the universe. While a typical region of this size should contain roughly 2,000 galaxies, astronomers have found only about 60 inside it. These few lonely galaxies are huddled together in a strange, tube-shaped strand running through the void's center. Scientists believe this cosmic hole formed when smaller voids merged over time. If our Milky Way had been placed in the center of the Boötes Void, humanity wouldn't have known other galaxies existed until the 1960s. This terrifying emptiness is a quiet monument in our universe's structure.
angle: If the Milky Way had been at the center of the Boötes Void, humanity wouldn't have known other galaxies existed until the 1960s instead of the 1920s.
disputed: BBC Sky at Night erroneously states the Boötes Void is 700 lightyears from Earth instead of 700 million lightyears. The script must ignore this error and use the 700 million lightyears figure supported by all other sources.

Some viral posts claim Barnard 68 is an empty void in space, but it is actually a dark nebula packed with stars that are simply obscured by dust in visible wavelengths. The script should clearly differentiate true cosmic voids from dark nebulae.

The exact size of the void ranges from 250 to 330 million light-years across, with some sources mentioning a radius of 200 million light-years (implying a 400 million light-year diameter). This occurs because voids have gradual, poorly-defined edges. The script should use the standard 330 million light-years across figure.
